meta.comment: engine.traffic (planned MOD) inc0 table (i): per-vehicle ESAL (Equivalent Single-Axle Load) factors from the AASHTO 4th-power axle-load law, plus the wear-accrual-to-repair-cost curve and repair trigger thresholds. This file is the sole OWNER of ESAL factors (referenced by scale_ladder.json's roadWearESALPerDay derivation and by vehicle_classes.json rows, never restated elsewhere -- GR#3).
meta.unitsConvention: esalFactor is dimensionless (equivalent standard 80kN/18,000lb single-axle-load passes per vehicle-km, AASHTO convention, normalised here so car=1 axle-load-equivalent per 100 vehicle-km -- see esalFactorBasis below for the exact normalisation); conditionIndex is 0(failed)-100(new) matching data/roads.json's implicit maintenance.conditionDecayPerMonth scale (referenced, not restated); repairCostMultiplier is dimensionless, applied to data/roads.json baseCostPounds (referenced, not restated).

esalFactorBasis.law: ESAL_ratio = (axleLoad_A / axleLoad_B)^4 (AASHTO Guide for Design of Pavement Structures, 1993, the '4th-power law' -- a doubling of axle load produces roughly a 16x increase in pavement damage per pass).
esalFactorBasis.normalisation: This table expresses esalFactor as damage PER VEHICLE-KM relative to a standard car (car = 1 reference axle-load-equivalent unit per 100 vehicle-km, i.e. car's esalFactor below of 0.0003 IS that reference unit scaled to a per-km basis matching scale_ladder.json's per-day rollup -- the absolute normalisation constant is this schema's own choice and is NOT independently meaningful outside this file's internal ratios; only the RATIOS between vehicle classes carry real-world grounding).
esalFactorBasis.source: AASHTO Guide for Design of Pavement Structures (1993), Appendix D load-equivalency-factor tables (typical single-unit truck ~2-3 ESAL/pass at legal axle loads, articulated combination trucks with multiple loaded axles commonly 5,000-15,000x a passenger car's per-pass damage depending on axle configuration and loading -- Aaron's brief anchor of '~10,000x' sits within this published range for a fully-loaded articulated HGV vs. a car).

car.source: AASHTO 4th-power law, car as the reference unit

motorbike.source: derived from AASHTO 4th-power law at motorbike axle load vs car

taxi.note: as car, slightly higher due to higher annual mileage/loading, not axle load

bus.source: derived from AASHTO 4th-power law at a loaded double-deck bus axle load vs car
bus.confidenceNote: the 4th-power LAW is literature; the specific bus axle-load figure used is this schema's own derived estimate

cargo_van.source: derived from AASHTO 4th-power law at a loaded van axle load vs car

rigid_truck.source: derived from AASHTO 4th-power law at a loaded rigid-HGV axle load vs car

articulated_truck.note: matches Aaron's brief anchor '~10,000x a car'
articulated_truck.source: AASHTO 4th-power law, calibrated to the brief's stated ratio

esalFactorVsRatioToCarPerPassReconciliat: BUG-932/BUG-917 r2 finding: articulated_truck's esalFactorPer100VehicleKm/car ratio is 6.0/0.0003 = 20000x, while ratioToCarPerPass is 10000x -- these are DELIBERATELY different metrics, not a typo: esalFactorPer100VehicleKm is damage per 100 VEHICLE-KM (distance-normalised, what roadWearStepOf actually consumes), while ratioToCarPerPass is damage per PASS (a single crossing, independent of distance) -- an articulated truck typically also travels further per trip than a car in this schema's implied trip-length mix, so the per-km ratio legitimately runs higher than the per-pass ratio. trafficWear.test.mjs's AC-4 explicitly pins that the module uses esalFactorPer100VehicleKm (the per-km law), never ratioToCarPerPass, and explicitly asserts the two ratios differ -- reconciling them to one number would silently break that structural pin. Recorded here (not changed) per the r3 lead amendment's 'one number, sourced' ask: the two numbers ARE each individually sourced (see esalFactorBasis above), they are simply not the SAME number by design.

railWear.$comment: Rail wear is a materially different mechanism (rolling contact fatigue / rail-head wear, not axle-load pavement flex) and is NOT modelled by the ESAL law. Placeholder flat per-train-km wear rate pending a dedicated rail-maintenance data pass (out of scope for inc0's road-wear table); tracked so engine.traffic does not silently assume rail is wear-free.

wearUnitsPerTrainKm.note: arbitrary internal unit, NOT AASHTO-comparable to esalFactorPer100VehicleKm above

conditionDecayPerESAL.note: LEGACY LITERAL, no longer the live source (BUG-932, FEAT-2326609800 inc7 r3): kept for backward documentation/validator coverage only. The engine's actual conditionDecayPerESAL constant is now DERIVED at load from targetTicksToResurfaceAtCapacity below (deriveConditionDecayPerEsalFrom), so the mechanic is calibrated to a stated in-game timescale rather than an independent hand-typed rate. conditionIndex points lost per cumulative ESAL unit absorbed by a road segment, on top of data/roads.json's existing time-based conditionDecayPerMonth (referenced, not restated) -- USE-driven decay is additive to age-driven decay, per the Blue-style brief ask ('the more a road is used the more repair it needs').
conditionDecayPerESAL.source: derived approximation calibrated so a busy A-road (avenue_2_plus_2, ~1800 pcu/h/lane sustained) needs a repair cycle on the order of months-to-a-few-years under continuous heavy use, matching the general shape of UK road-maintenance funding cycles

targetTicksToResurfaceAtCapacity.note: BUG-932 (FEAT-2326609800 inc7 r3 lead amendment): ticks for a segment held at referenceVehiclesPerTickAtCapacity's continuous car-equivalent flow (over a 1km reference segment) to accrue enough ESAL to fall from conditionIndex 100 to wearToRepairCost.repairTriggerConditionIndex (60) -- i.e. this is what makes the mechanic LIVE under a stated timescale instead of an inert hand-typed rate; conditionDecayPerESAL is derived FROM this field at load (deriveConditionDecayPerEsalFrom), not the other way round.
targetTicksToResurfaceAtCapacity.referenceVehiclesPerTickAtCapacitySource: placeholder order-of-magnitude for a busy single-lane arterial's continuous car-equivalent vehicle flow per tick; balance regime, pending Aaron's pass -- matches this file's existing placeholder/derived provenance convention (chosen to avoid coupling the load-time derivation to the scale-ladder's runtime-only peakHourFactor, which cannot be resolved at module-load time)
targetTicksToResurfaceAtCapacity.source: derived: 4320 ticks (~12 real-world months at the game's existing TICKS_PER_MONTH convention referenced elsewhere in this schema, matching conditionDecayPerESAL's original note about a months-to-a-few-years repair cycle under continuous heavy use)

repairTriggerConditionIndex.note: below this conditionIndex a segment is flagged repair-due; matches the general shape of UK road-condition surveys' 'poor' category threshold (mapping sanity-check only, not a literal DfT road-condition-survey cut-off)
repairTriggerConditionIndex.source: derived approximation, order-of-magnitude cross-check against UK road-condition survey category bands

repairCostCurve.note: repair-trigger threshold; cost multiplier applies to data/roads.json baseCostPounds for that class (referenced, not restated)
approaching full-reconstruction cost territory rather than resurfacing
failed pavement; full rebuild, matches roughly data/roads.json upgrade.rebuildDisruptionPermille order-of-magnitude (referenced, not restated)

wearToRepairCost.interpolationRule: Piecewise-linear interpolation between the listed conditionIndex anchor points.
wearToRepairCost.source: Derived approximation; the SHAPE (convex, cost accelerates sharply below the repair-trigger threshold) follows standard pavement-management 'worse-first-costs-more' literature (e.g. World Bank HDM-4 pavement deterioration modelling convention, cited for shape only, not for these specific multiplier values).

provenance.source: AASHTO Guide for Design of Pavement Structures (1993, 4th-power law) for esalFactorBasis; remaining figures derived approximations calibrated to Aaron's brief anchor (articulated HGV ~10,000x a car) and general pavement-management literature shape
provenance.note: The 4TH-POWER LAW itself is literature-grounded and load-bearing; the specific per-vehicle-class ratios and the repair-cost curve are directional placeholders pending Aaron's balance pass.
